slides.text: For five years, I constructed the Thursday crossword puzzle for the city paper, and for five years, the only person who ever solved it in ink without a single smudge was the woman at the corner table of Café Lumière. I knew her habits by heart: she bit her lower lip on the pun clues, ordered a cortado at 8:10 AM, and smiled whenever I snuck an astronomy word into the grid.

I was too shy to interrupt her mornings, so I started building the puzzles for an audience of one. When she looked sad on a rainy week in April, 14-Across was 'Passages after storms (8 letters): RAINBOWS.' When she wore a vintage emerald scarf, 28-Down was 'Color that suits the corner table (5 letters): GREEN.' One morning I watched her pause, her pen hovering over the paper as she slowly looked around the café.

The next Thursday, I staked everything on the centerpiece clue, 42-Across: 'Question from the man in the blue sweater by the espresso bar (4, 3, 5, 2): WILL YOU MARRY ME?' No—too fast. I changed it to: 'HAVE TEA WITH ME.' At 8:17 AM, she walked over to my table, laid the newspaper down between us, and pointed to the margin where she had drawn four new squares in bold black ink: 'Y-E-S-S.'
